name: Sam Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Sam, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on Larkfield Rise, a new estate of a hundred and twenty houses out past the ring road, working for a joinery subcontractor. Right now it's second fix, so skirting, architraves, hanging internal doors, and I'm slow, I'll admit it. Bogdan, the joiner I'm under, can do a house of skirting in a day and I take nearly two. I started on the tools at fifty-four, after twenty-six years driving a forklift at a supermarket warehouse.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why did you leave the warehouse?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The robots came. They put in those shuttle systems, little carts that run up and down the racks on their own, and within a year they needed a third of the drivers. I took the redundancy money, and most of it went on my daughter Efua's wedding and the car, so we've got next to nothing put by now. My wife Abena does school dinners, and between us we cover the rent and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the computers write the emails and leave the doors to us. At break I'd probably joke to Bogdan that I'd retrained for nothing, because I was so sure the robots were coming here too. Online, I'd maybe share something saying the money should go into apprenticeships instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd breathe out. I watched machines take my last job, so part of me has been waiting for it to happen again. If it doesn't, then I just have to get faster at skirting and I'm fine for my last few working years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Larkfield and keep at my level two joinery certificate at the college. I'd use the chat app my son put on my phone now and then, like I do for working out stair measurements, but that's it. And I'd finally join the builders' union, because there's no union on this site and I miss having one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A bit of relief, like when the hospital says the test came back clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you miss having a union so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the warehouse I was a shop steward for nine years, and when the shuttles came we got people an extra month's pay and kept the older drivers on the loading bays. Here, I'm on day rate through a subcontractor, and if they don't need me Monday, they just don't ring. Nobody to talk to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd joke you retrained for nothing. Would that feel like a waste?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. Somebody's always going to need doors hung, and I like going home with sawdust on my boots instead of diesel on my hands. It's slower money than the forklift, but it's honest.

S0.say: I'd say good, let computers do the emails and leave the doors to us. I'd joke I retrained for nothing and say the money should go into apprenticeships.
S0.think: I'd breathe out, because I've been waiting for machines to take a second job off me. Without that, I just need to get faster at skirting.
S0.do: Carries on at the Larkfield Rise estate and keeps working towards his level two joinery certificate. Uses the chat app on his phone now and then and joins the builders' union.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like getting a clear test result.
S0.quote: If it doesn't, then I just have to get faster at skirting and I'm fine for my last few working years.
S0.fieldNote: Sam has lived through automation once, which makes this picture feel like a reprieve rather than a letdown. He misses the union badly and links it directly to how the warehouse job losses were handled. He uses AI lightly and practically, for stair maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've seen this film before, and the ending depends on who's in the room. I'd tell people at work that the warehouse changed over three years and the ones who had a union came out better. I'd say it online too, though only my nephew reads what I write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right for a while, because a building site is mud and mess, not a flat warehouse floor. But the planning, the ordering, the measuring would all go onto tablets, and I'm not quick with that. It's not the robot I fear, it's being the slowest one with the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Bogdan to show me whatever app they bring in and I'd practise at home at night with my son Kwame, who fixes buses and is good with this stuff. I'd get the union to push for the subcontractors to pay for the training, not us. I'd try to put twenty-five a week aside, which means no more Saturday football at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but I know the shape of it. It's not new to me, so it's not as frightening as the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the first time, at the warehouse, that you'd do differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I waited. I thought I'm a good driver, they'll keep me, and I didn't learn the control screens when they offered the course. The ones who did ended up supervising the shuttles. I won't make that mistake twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Giving up the Saturday football at the pub, is that a big thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my one afternoon out. Me, my brother-in-law and two old drivers from the warehouse, a pint each and the match on the big screen. But I'd rather lose that than get caught short again, and I can watch it at home with Abena complaining.

S1.say: I'd say I've seen this film before and the ending depends on who's in the room. At the warehouse, the people with a union came out better.
S1.think: A building site is too messy for robots to take over quickly, but the planning and measuring would move onto tablets. What I fear is being the slowest one with the new tools, not the robot itself.
S1.do: Asks his lead joiner to show him new apps and practises at home with his son. Pushes the union to make subcontractors pay for training and saves about twenty-five a week by dropping Saturday football at the pub.
S1.feel: Uneasy but familiar, less frightening than the first time.
S1.quote: It's not the robot I fear, it's being the slowest one with the new tools.
S1.fieldNote: Sam's past regret drives his plan: he skipped the control-screen course at the warehouse and watched others get promoted. This time he'd learn the tools early, with his son's help. He still treats the union as the main way to make change fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this time it's not a few hundred drivers, it's everyone, so the government has to act like it's a war. I'd say we need a basic income, paid by taxing the companies that own the robots. And I'd be telling people at work to join the union now, today, not next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in real trouble. In 2028 I'm sixty, and if robots are hanging doors on Larkfield there's no warehouse to go back to either, because the robots already have that. Abena's school dinners won't cover the rent on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Abena and cut everything we can, the car, the phone deals, the satellite TV, maybe two hundred a month. I'd ask about any job looking after the robots on site, like clearing up after them or moving materials, because I know how those machines break down. And I'd go to every union meeting and every march, because in two years nothing gets done unless people are loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like being back in that warehouse canteen when the manager came in with his folder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really try for a job looking after the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would. When the shuttles jammed at the warehouse, it was us old drivers who knew where to look, which rail, which sensor was dirty. Maybe a site would want someone like that, someone who knows the building and knows the machines go wrong. I don't know if they'd pay much, but it's better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you do in the time before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get every bit of paper sorted, my joinery card, my forklift licence renewed, anything that proves I can do something. I'd ask Bogdan to let me do the harder jobs now, stairs and door sets, so I'm worth keeping a bit longer. And I'd tell Abena we stop pretending we'll have a holiday next year.

S2.say: I'd say it's not a few hundred drivers this time, it's everyone, so the government must act as if it's a war. We'd need a basic income paid by taxing robot owners, and everyone should join a union now.
S2.think: I'd be in real trouble at sixty, with no warehouse to go back to because robots have that too. Abena's school dinners wage won't cover the rent on its own.
S2.do: Cuts the car, phone deals and satellite TV to save about two hundred a month. Asks about jobs looking after the site robots and goes to every union meeting and march.
S2.feel: A bit sick, like waiting for the manager with the folder in the warehouse canteen.
S2.quote: When the shuttles jammed at the warehouse, it was us old drivers who knew where to look, which rail, which sensor was dirty.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture, Sam reaches for something he knows: robots break down and someone has to understand them. He's frightened about rent but keeps looking for a role rather than giving up. His politics sharpen into a call for a basic income funded by robot owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do it properly if they start tomorrow. I'd push the union to get a deal for older workers: either retraining on the robots, or an early pension. That's what I'd say at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gets me to sixty-three, and that's close enough to the pension that I could maybe bridge it. If I can stay on the tools till sixty-one and then get something looking after the machines, I'd make it. Two years was a cliff, five is a steep hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for any short course on robot maintenance or site machinery the college or the union runs, even if it's evenings after a full day. I'd keep the twenty-five a week going and add any overtime on top. And I'd talk to Abena about whether we could move somewhere cheaper in a few years, maybe nearer Efua.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I feel like I've got hands on the wheel. There's time to do something, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to learn before I need it, not after. In the warehouse I learned the hard way that you get the training before the machines arrive or you don't get it at all. With five years, I can be the one they call when the robot's stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move nearer your daughter. How would she feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Efua would be pleased, I think, because she's got a baby on the way and she'd want help. Abena would see the grandchild every day. It's me who'd find it hardest, leaving the town I've lived in for thirty years.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if they start tomorrow. I'd push the union for a deal for older workers, either robot retraining or an early pension.
S3.think: Five years gets me to sixty-three, near enough to the pension that I could maybe bridge it. Two years was a cliff; five is a steep hill.
S3.do: Signs up for any evening course on robot maintenance or site machinery and keeps saving twenty-five a week plus overtime. Talks with his wife about moving somewhere cheaper, nearer their daughter, in a few years.
S3.feel: Worried, but with his hands on the wheel because there's time to act.
S3.quote: Two years was a cliff, five is a steep hill.
S3.fieldNote: For Sam the extra time matters a great deal: it lets him get training before the machines arrive, which is the lesson he took from the warehouse. He'd study in the evenings despite tiredness. His plan mixes union pressure with personal retraining, which fits his steady, proven-first approach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we shouldn't waste it arguing. I'd want every apprenticeship to include working with the machines from now on. And I'd want the government to promise that nobody over fifty-five gets thrown out with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years and I'm sixty-eight, past the pension age. So I'd probably finish on the tools, or near enough, and the machines would come for the young ones more than me. I'd be worried for Kwame, honestly, because buses will drive themselves too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the joinery and get my level two, and take one of those robot courses later on, once I've seen they're real. I'd save what I can, and I'd write to my local politician asking for a plan for workers, which I've never done before. Otherwise I'd mostly carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. I'd be fine, probably, but it's my boys I'd lie awake about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kwame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him what I wish someone had told me at the warehouse: learn the machine that's going to replace you, and learn it first. He's thirty, he's got time. And keep his union card, because that's what saved the older drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd write to a politician for the first time. What would the letter say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a fifty-eight-year-old joiner who already lost one job to robots, and I'd like to know your plan before I lose the second. Short and polite. I'd probably get Kwame to help me type it, or ask the chat app to tidy the spelling.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and every apprenticeship should include working with the machines. The government should promise no one over fifty-five is thrown out with nothing.
S4.think: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, past pension age, so I'd probably finish on the tools or near enough. I'd worry more for Kwame, because buses will drive themselves too.
S4.do: Finishes his level two joinery and takes a robot course once he's seen it's real. Saves what he can and writes to his local politician for the first time asking for a plan for workers.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, mostly for his sons.
S4.quote: I'd tell him what I wish someone had told me at the warehouse: learn the machine that's going to replace you, and learn it first.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Sam's personal fear fades because he'd reach pension age, and his worry moves to his son. He'd still wait to see the robot courses are real before signing up. Writing to a politician would be a first for him, which shows how seriously he'd take it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I've been through a slow version of this and it nearly broke us, so a fast one with nothing saved would be terrible. What would help is training on the machines before they arrive, paid by the companies, and a guarantee for older workers, an early pension or a job minding the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it felt like the first time. When I handed in my forklift licence card, I sat in the car park for an hour before I could drive home. I don't want to sit in that car park again at sixty.

headlineQuote: I don't want to sit in that car park again at sixty.
portrait: Sam Mensah is a 58-year-old improver joiner on a new housing estate who came into building after robots cut his forklift job at a supermarket warehouse. A former shop steward, he misses having a union and sees every scenario through the lens of that first loss. He's calm if AI stalls, uneasy under steady change, and alarmed by fast AGI, but he keeps looking for a role minding the machines because he knows they break down. With five or ten years, he'd train early, save a little and shift his worry to his sons.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he's lived through a slow version of job loss already and has nothing saved for a fast one.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid training on the machines before they arrive and a guarantee for older workers, either an early pension or a job minding the robots.
